messages.subject: Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
parts:
Hi,

Is it correct that INLA does not have the option to model correlation between Gaussian residuals?
Instead of using random effects to model the correlation between measurements I would like to model the correlation between measurements using residuals.

Hereby attached is an example model using nlme:
library(nlme)
set.seed(2021)
#Total of N individuals
N<-10
#n=3 correlated measurements per individual
n<-3
data<-data.frame(id=rep(1:N, each=n), y=NA, x=NA)
#setting up data such that the 3 measurements on 1 individual are correlated
for (i in 1:N){
  data$x[(3*(i-1)+1):(3*i)]<-rnorm(1)+rnorm(n, sd=0.1)
}
#Creating response
data$y<-3+2*data$x+rnorm(n*N, sd=0.5)
#fitting using gls with correlated residuals
fm1 <- gls(y ~ 1 + x, data=data,
           correlation = corSymm(form = ~ 1 | id))
#Obtain covariance matrix of correlated residuals
cov2cor(getVarCov(fm1, individual = 1))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
parts:
INLA only support conditional independent data, but for Gaussian
response, you can always just expand the latent field (or linear
predictor) to have define dependent data. sometimes this involve setting
the likelihood to have fixed high precision, like having AR1
depenendency in the observations.

in these cases, you'll end up with a 'fake' linear predictor, for which
a subset of it, is the real one.

there are also generic iid models in dimension up to 10, with general
covariance structure, that can be used for this (see inla.doc("iidkd")
for a new testing version)

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Correlated Gaussian residuals in INLA
parts:
Hi,

This is a different model than the first one. In the first you have correlated residuals, now you have correlated residuals (u_ij) and an additional one (e_ij). This may lead to identifiability issues.

For the first model you asked, the 'iid3d' model in INLA may be considered and so all the three variances are already fitted by this latent model, thus with no likelihood variances needed.

best regards,
Elias

This model should be straight forward, and its weird you do not get the
correlation and sigma_{b2} correct. There is no confounding going on,
right, like with with noise variances? You still get it wrong if you
fix the likelihoods to be Gaussians with known precisions?

I guess you do simulations so you can chose i=1..I, and j=1..J, and its
still bad even with large I and J ?

The 'iid2d' model use directly the (transformed) correlation as the
hyperparameter, hence you should get it directly out in the results.

Can you retry the same model without all covariates, ie just the iid2d
model? This is also one of the examples in inla.doc('iid2d')

There is a recent implementation, 'iidkd' that scales better for higher
'k', which uses a different parameterisation, but this should not change
anything for dimension 2.

Best

Here is the result and the code for 200 individuals each with 5 time repeated measures.
INLA worked perfectly well for the fixed estimates and residuals.

```
inla_sim <- function(seed,
                     nid = 200, # num of individuals
                     eachid = 5, # visit num for each individual
                     sigma_bx, # random effect for the first outcome
                     lambda, # scaled up for hte second outcome
                     rho, # correlation between the two outcomes
                     sigma_ex = 1, # residual for the first outcome
                     sigma_ey = 0.5, # residual for the second outcome
                     ## add intercepts
                     InterceptX,
                     InterceptY){
  set.seed(seed)

  n = eachid * nid
  id <- rep(1:200, each = 5)
  # browser()
  ## sigma_y is a scaled sigma_x
  sigma_by <- lambda * sigma_bx
  Sigma <- matrix(data = c(sigma_bx^2, rho * sigma_bx * sigma_by,
                           rho * sigma_bx * sigma_by, sigma_by^2),
                  nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  errorX <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma_ex)
  errorY <- rnorm(n, 0, sigma_ey)
 
  randomXY <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = nid,
                            mu = c(0, 0),
                            Sigma = Sigma) %>%
    as.data.frame()
 
  ## the outcomes in two different cols
  y <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
  y[1:n, 1] <- InterceptX + randomXY[id, 1] + errorX
  y[n + 1:n, 2] <- InterceptY  + randomXY[id, 2] + errorY
 
  ## indicator intercept cols
  I <- matrix(NA, nrow = 2 * n, ncol = 2)
  I[1:n, 1] <- 1
  I[n + 1:n, 2] <- 1

  ## different ways for setting up ids
  idex <- rep(1:2, each = n)
  idx <- as.numeric(c(id, rep(NA, n)))
  idy <- as.numeric(c(rep(NA, n), as.numeric(id) + nid))
  idxy <- as.numeric(c(id, as.numeric(id) + nid))
 
  data71 <- list(y = y, I = I,
                 idxy = idxy,
                 idex = idex,
                 idx = idx, idy = idy)
 
  ## independent random effects
  sim.joint0 <- y ~  -1 + I +
    f(idx, model = "iid") +
    f(idy, model = "iid")
 
 
  ## unstructured jmm
sim.joint1 <- y ~  -1 + I +

f(idxy, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0))))
## pairwised jmm with fixed scale
sim.joint2 <- y ~  -1 + I +

f(idx, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +

f(idy, copy = "idx", fixed = TRUE)
 
 
  ## pairwised jmm with new beta scale to the second outcome
  sim.joint3 <- y ~  -1 + I +

f(idx, model = "iid2d", n = 2 * n,
      hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(4, 0.001, 0.001, 0)))) +
    f(idy, copy = "idx", fixed = FALSE)
inla.joint0 <- try(inla(sim.joint0,
family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
# control.family = list(initial = 10),

# control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))
  inla.joint1 <- try(inla(sim.joint1,
                     family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
                     # control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))
inla.joint2 <- try(inla(sim.joint2,
family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
# control.family = list(initial = 10),

# control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))
inla.joint3 <- try(inla(sim.joint3,
family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
# control.family = list(initial = 10),

# control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                     # control.compute = list(dic = TRUE),
                     data = data71))

cat(paste0("number ", seed, " iteration is done \n"))

  return(list(inla_1 = inla.joint1,
              inla_2 = inla.joint2,
              inla_0 = inla.joint0,
              inla_3 = inla.joint3,
              true_cov = Sigma,
              error_cov = cov(cbind(errorX, errorY)),
              sample_cov = cov(randomXY),
              sample_cor = cor(randomXY)))
}


Randy
```

This model should be straight forward, and its weird you do not get the
correlation and sigma_{b2} correct. There is no confounding going on,
right, like with with noise variances? You still get it wrong if you
fix the likelihoods to be Gaussians with known precisions?

I guess you do simulations so you can chose i=1..I, and j=1..J, and its
still bad even with large I and J ?

The 'iid2d' model use directly the (transformed) correlation as the
hyperparameter, hence you should get it directly out in the results.

Can you retry the same model without all covariates, ie just the iid2d
model? This is also one of the examples in inla.doc('iid2d')

There is a recent implementation, 'iidkd' that scales better for higher
'k', which uses a different parameterisation, but this should not change
anything for dimension 2.

Best
H
